analysis.one_liner: Taxes sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide pollution from power plants by the pound.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 2 cosponsors, was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee in March 1990 and died there without a hearing or any vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would charge electric utilities a tax for every pound of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide their plants release into the air, starting at 15 cents and 10 cents per pound in 1991 and rising to 45 cents and 30 cents by 1997, adjusted for inflation. It would tighten the exemption levels over time and hold brand-new plants to much stricter limits, so the cheapest way to avoid the tax would be to burn cleaner fuel or install pollution controls. Small power producers under 75 megawatts would be exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live downwind of coal- and oil-fired power plants — the people who breathe the smog and whose lakes, forests, and buildings take the acid rain that sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide cause. The tax would give utilities a direct financial reason to cut emissions, since every pound avoided is money saved.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities downwind of coal-fired power plants

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a per-pound excise tax on sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide from electric utility generating units, with rates that climb from 15 cents and 10 cents per pound in 1991 to 45 cents and 30 cents in 1997 and after, and rise further with inflation.
Makes the tax fall directly on each unit's operator, and requires emissions to be measured with continuous monitoring devices, so utilities could not avoid it by underestimating pollution.

Tightens the untaxed exemption level every few years — from 1.2 pounds of sulfur dioxide per million Btu of fuel in the mid-1990s down to 0.6 pounds after 1999 — and sets a much stricter threshold (0.25 pounds) for any plant built after the law's enactment, pushing new construction toward cleaner fuel and pollution controls from day one.

Would have funded the cleanup through the polluters themselves rather than through general tax revenue, and shields very small producers (units under 75 megawatts run by operators with at most 150 megawatts total) from the cost.

analysis.who_pays: The operators of large fossil-fuel power plants, who would pay the tax per pound of emissions, and their customers, since utilities would pass some or all of the cost through to electricity bills. The heaviest burden would fall on plants burning high-sulfur coal and on the coal regions that supply them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal-burning utilities, their customers, coal regions

drawbacks.text: Utilities would pass much of the tax through to electricity bills, so households — including lower-income households in coal-dependent states — would pay part of the cost of cleaner air in their monthly rates.

The design leaves substantial pollution untaxed: emissions below the exemption level cost nothing, operators could use fuel-based estimates instead of monitors before 1993, and small operators are entirely exempt, so some plants would keep polluting for free.

An honest supporter would acknowledge the cost lands unevenly: plants burning high-sulfur coal would owe far more than cleaner plants, concentrating the burden on Midwest and Appalachian utility customers and coal-mining communities rather than spreading it nationally.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A tax charged by the pound of pollution is the most direct way to make the parties causing acid rain and smog pay for it, and the rising rates and shrinking exemptions are built to keep pushing emissions down. The real cost is higher electricity prices passed through to customers, concentrated in coal-burning regions. The bill was a live alternative in the same debate that produced the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990, which took the different approach of capping total sulfur dioxide emissions and letting utilities trade permits; this bill never got considered alongside it. On the merits it was a straightforward polluter-pays measure with a real but uneven consumer cost, and the public never got to see it debated.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Represent Pete Stark introduced the bill on March 5, 1990, joined by Representative Thomas Downey, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which handles tax legislation.
That referral was the last action of any kind — the committee never held a hearing, marked it up, or voted, and the bill never reached the House floor.
The 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, and the bill expired with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal-burning electric utilities and their coal suppliers, who never faced a per-pound tax on their emissions; the people downwind continued to absorb the pollution instead.

for.name: Rep. Fortney Pete Stark
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to tax sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions from utility plants.

for.name: Rep. Thomas Downey
for.what_they_did: Joined Stark in introducing the bill.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Dan Rostenkowski (D-IL)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan split is unknown; the only record is that the sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats among the 257 House Democrats.

industries.note: The bill would charge these plants by the pound for the sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide they emit, with rates that keep rising and exemption thresholds that keep tightening. Their cheapest escape — burning cleaner fuel or installing scrubbers — is exactly the outcome the public wanted, so their financial interest ran against the bill's purpose.

industries.industry: Coal mining, especially high-sulfur coal producers
industries.note: A per-pound emissions tax would push utilities away from high-sulfur coal toward low-sulfur coal or other fuels, shrinking the market for the dirtiest coal. Low-sulfur western producers could have gained, but the tax's pressure would fall hardest on high-sulfur mining regions.
